html:
For a century, from 1221 to 1327, Mongol armies raided north India again and again. The Delhi Sultanate held them off, which made it one of the few states to do so.

It began when Genghis Khan chased the prince of Khwarazm to the Indus in 1221 (see the Battle of the Indus) and then turned back. From the 1240s Mongol forces based in Afghanistan raided Punjab most years. They sacked Lahore in 1241. Sultan Balban built a line of forts and lost his eldest son in battle against them in 1285.

The great attacks came from the Chagatai Khanate between 1297 and 1306, in the reign of Alauddin Khalji:

  • 1299: a large army marched on Delhi and was beaten at Kili, just outside the city.
  • 1303: another besieged Delhi for two months while the sultan sheltered in his camp at Siri.
  • 1305 and 1306: two more were destroyed, and the prisoners were trampled by elephants.

The last big raid reached the Delhi region in 1327.

The threat shaped the sultanate. It kept a huge cavalry army, taxed heavily to pay for it, and took in scholars and craftsmen fleeing the Mongols from Iran and Central Asia. In 1398 Timur, a Turco-Mongol conqueror, did what the Mongols had not.
sum: For a century, from 1221 to 1327, Mongol armies raided north India again and again. The Delhi Sultanate held them off, which made it one of the few states to do so.
